title: Techniques for Solving Exponential Equations
overview: Not every exponential equation has a convenient common base. In this section you take the logarithm of both sides, use the power law to bring the variable down, and handle tougher equations that turn into quadratics — watching out for **extraneous roots**. Along the way you will model radioactive decay, depreciation and the sustain of a guitar note.
objectives: Solve exponential equations by taking the common logarithm of both sides
Give exact answers in terms of logarithms and decimal approximations
Determine half-lives and decay times using $A = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$
Solve equations with different bases on each side by collecting and factoring
Solve exponential equations of quadratic form and reject extraneous roots

lessons.title: When there is no common base: take the logarithm of both sides
lessons.body:
Some equations have no convenient common base, such as $1.07^t = 2$ or $4^{2x-1} = 3^{x+2}$. The fix is to take the **common logarithm of both sides**. An equation stays balanced when you do the same thing to both sides, as long as both sides are positive.

The **power law of logarithms**, $\log x^n = n\log x$, then brings the variable down out of the exponent.

**Example:** solve $2 = 1.07^t$.

$$\log 2 = \log 1.07^t \;\Rightarrow\; \log 2 = t\log 1.07 \;\Rightarrow\; t = \frac{\log 2}{\log 1.07} \approx 10.24$$

> **Exact vs approximate.** $t = \frac{\log 2}{\log 1.07}$ is the **exact** answer. $10.24$ is an approximation. When a question says "exact", leave the logarithms in.

**Isolate the power first.** For $100 = 10(1.04)^t$, divide by 10 before taking logarithms: $10 = 1.04^t$, so $t = \frac{\log 10}{\log 1.04} = \frac{1}{\log 1.04} \approx 58.7$.

lessons.title: Radioactive decay and half-life
lessons.body:
The **half-life** of a radioactive substance is the time it takes for half of a sample to decay. The amount remaining is

$$A(t) = A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{\frac{t}{h}}$$

* $A_0$ — the initial amount
* $h$ — the half-life (same time unit as $t$)
* $\frac{t}{h}$ — the number of half-lives that have passed; each one multiplies the amount by $\frac12$

After one half-life ($t = h$) half remains; after two ($t = 2h$) a quarter remains; and so on.

**Finding the half-life from data.** Polonium-218: 100 mg becomes 80 mg after 1 min.

$$80 = 100\left(\tfrac12\right)^{\frac1h} \;\Rightarrow\; 0.8 = 0.5^{\frac1h} \;\Rightarrow\; \log 0.8 = \tfrac1h\log 0.5 \;\Rightarrow\; h = \frac{\log 0.5}{\log 0.8} \approx 3.1 \text{ min}$$

```plot
title: Polonium-218: A(t) = 100(1/2)^(t/3.1)
f: 100*0.5^(x/3.1) | label=A(t), mg
domain: 0, 15
range: 0, 110
ticks: 3.1, 25
points: (3.1, 50), (6.2, 25), (9.3, 12.5)
asymptote y: 0
```

The marked points show the amount halving every 3.1 min. The curve approaches 0 but never reaches it.

The same model describes anything that halves at a steady rate: the value of a car or computer, the loudness of a guitar note as it fades, caffeine in your blood.

lessons.title: Different bases on both sides
lessons.body:
To solve $4^{2x-1} = 3^{x+2}$:

1. Take the common logarithm of both sides: $\log 4^{2x-1} = \log 3^{x+2}$.
2. Apply the power law: $(2x-1)\log 4 = (x+2)\log 3$.
3. Expand: $2x\log4 - \log 4 = x\log 3 + 2\log 3$.
4. Collect the $x$-terms on one side: $2x\log 4 - x\log 3 = 2\log 3 + \log 4$.
5. Factor out $x$: $x(2\log 4 - \log 3) = 2\log 3 + \log 4$.
6. Divide: $x = \dfrac{2\log 3 + \log 4}{2\log 4 - \log 3} \approx 2.14$.

> $\log 4$ and $\log 3$ are just **numbers** (about 0.602 and 0.477). Treat them like coefficients: collect, factor and divide.

```plot
title: y = 4^(2x-1) and y = 3^(x+2) intersect near x = 2.14
f: 4^(2*x-1) | label=y = 4^(2x − 1)
f: 3^(x+2) | label=y = 3^(x + 2)
domain: 0, 3
range: 0, 150
ticks: 0.5, 25
points: (2.1397, 94.6)
```

lessons.title: Equations of quadratic form
lessons.body:
Some exponential equations hide a quadratic. Look for $b^{2x}$, which is $(b^x)^2$.

**Example:** $2^{2x} + 2^x - 6 = 0$. Let $z = 2^x$:

$$z^2 + z - 6 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (z+3)(z-2) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; z = -3 \text{ or } z = 2$$

* $2^x = 2$ gives $x = 1$ ✓
* $2^x = -3$ is impossible, because $2^x > 0$ for every real $x$. This root is **extraneous**: reject it.

**Example:** $2^x - 2^{-x} = 4$. Multiply both sides by $2^x$ (remember $2^x\cdot2^{-x} = 2^0 = 1$):

$$2^{2x} - 1 = 4(2^x) \;\Rightarrow\; z^2 - 4z - 1 = 0, \quad z = 2^x$$

The quadratic formula gives $z = 2 \pm \sqrt5$. Since $2 - \sqrt5 < 0$, reject it. From $2^x = 2 + \sqrt 5$, $x = \frac{\log(2+\sqrt5)}{\log 2} \approx 2.08$.

> Multiplying both sides by an expression that contains the variable can **introduce extraneous roots**. Always check each root in the original equation.

lessons.title: Extraneous roots and equations with no solution
lessons.body:
An **extraneous root** is a value produced by a correct-looking algebraic process that does **not** satisfy the original equation.

For exponential equations they usually appear when a substitution $z = b^x$ leads to $z \le 0$. A positive base raised to any real power is always positive, so

$$b^x = \text{(negative number or 0)} \quad\text{has no solution.}$$

**No real solutions at all.** Does $4^{2x} + 2(4^x) + 3 = 0$ have a solution? Every term on the left is positive, so the sum can never be 0. In quadratic form, $z^2 + 2z + 3 = 0$ has discriminant $4 - 12 < 0$, so there are no real $z$ values either.

**How to check**

* Substitute each candidate into the **original** equation, or
* graph both sides and look for intersections. The number of intersection points equals the number of real solutions.

lessons.title: Applications: decay, depreciation and growth
lessons.body:
| Situation | Model | Unknown you might solve for |
|---|---|---|
| Radioactive decay | $A = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{h}}$ | half-life $h$, or time $t$ |
| Depreciating car | $V = V_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{h}}$ | time to reach a value |
| Doubling audience | $N = N_0(2)^t$ | when two audiences are equal |
| Advertising response | $P = 1 - 2^{-0.05n}$ | days until $P$ passes a target |
| Guitar sustain | $I = I_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{12}}$ | time for the note to fade |

**Strategy for any word problem**

1. Write the model and substitute the known values.
2. **Isolate the power** (divide by the coefficient, move constants).
3. Take the logarithm of both sides and apply the power law.
4. Solve, round sensibly, and answer in a sentence with units.
5. Ask whether the answer is reasonable (for example, a time should be positive).

keyTerms.definition: The time required for an amount to decay to half of its initial value. In $A = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$ it is $h$.
$\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$ for $b>0,\ b\ne1,\ x>0$. It moves an exponent down into a product.
An answer left in terms of logarithms or radicals, e.g. $x = \frac{\log 5}{\log 3}$.
A value obtained while solving that does not satisfy the original equation and must be rejected.
An equation such as $b^{2x} + p\,b^x + q = 0$ that becomes a quadratic when $z = b^x$.
The process by which an unstable element changes into another element, releasing energy. The amount left follows an exponential model.

formulas.name: Half-life from data
formulas.meaning: Rearranged from the model after taking logarithms.

formulas.name: Quadratic formula
formulas.meaning: Use it when $z = b^x$ gives a quadratic that does not factor; reject any $z \le 0$.

workedExamples.title: Find a half-life
workedExamples.problem: One minute after a 100-mg sample of polonium-218 is placed in a chamber, 80 mg remains. Determine the half-life.
workedExamples.answer: The half-life of polonium-218 is about 3.1 min.

workedExamples.title: Different bases
workedExamples.problem: Solve $4^{2x-1} = 3^{x+2}$. Give an exact answer and a decimal approximation.

workedExamples.title: Quadratic form with the quadratic formula
steps: $2 - \sqrt5 < 0$ is impossible for $2^x$, so reject it.

workedExamples.title: Factorable quadratic form
steps: Both values of $z$ are positive, so neither root is extraneous.

workedExamples.title: Depreciation
workedExamples.problem: A minivan bought for 24 000 dollars has value $V(t) = 24\,000\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac t3}$, where $t$ is in years. When is it worth 10% of its purchase price?

misconceptions.fact: The power law applies only to an exponent. Isolate the power first ($1.04^t = \ldots$) or use $\log(ab) = \log a + \log b$.
A **quotient of logarithms** is not the logarithm of a quotient. Evaluate the top and bottom separately: $\frac{0.3010}{0.0294} \approx 10.24$.

misconceptions.myth: Both roots of the quadratic in $z$ give solutions.
misconceptions.fact: Each $z$ must equal $b^x > 0$. Any $z \le 0$ gives an **extraneous** root.

misconceptions.myth: Half-life means the substance is gone after two half-lives.
misconceptions.fact: After two half-lives a **quarter** remains, after three an eighth. Exponential decay never reaches zero.

misconceptions.myth: $2^x - 2^{-x} = 4$ can be solved by taking logs: $x\log 2 - (-x)\log 2 = \log 4$.
misconceptions.fact: The logarithm of a **difference** cannot be split: $\log(a-b) \ne \log a - \log b$. Use the quadratic-form method instead.

realWorld.title: Carbon and medical isotopes
realWorld.body: Hospitals use short-lived isotopes for imaging. Knowing the half-life lets technicians calculate how much tracer remains when a scan begins.

realWorld.title: Car and computer depreciation
realWorld.body: Many items lose value by a constant percentage each year. Solving $V = V_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$ tells you when the item reaches a trade-in value.

realWorld.title: Guitar sustain
realWorld.body: A plucked string's intensity fades exponentially. Guitar designers compare 'sustain' by the time for the intensity to fall to a fraction of its starting value.

realWorld.title: Viral content
realWorld.body: A video whose audience doubles daily follows $N = N_0\cdot2^t$. Comparing two such models (one doubling, one tripling) means solving an equation with different bases.

practice.question: Solve for $t$ to two decimal places: (a) $2 = 1.07^t$ (b) $3 = 1.1^t$
practice.hint: Take the common logarithm of both sides.

practice.question: A 20-mg sample of thorium-233 decays to 17 mg after 5 min. Find the half-life.
Does $4^{2x} + 2(4^x) + 3 = 0$ have a real solution?
practice.hint: What is the sign of each term?
practice.solution: No. Each term is positive for every real $x$, so the left side is always greater than 3. (Also $z^2+2z+3=0$ has a negative discriminant.)

summary: Taking the common logarithm of both sides keeps an equation balanced and, with the power law, brings the variable out of the exponent.
Isolate the power before taking logarithms.
Half-life model: $A = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$; solve for $h$ or $t$ with logarithms.
With different bases: apply the power law, expand, collect the variable terms, factor and divide.
Equations such as $b^{2x} + pb^x + q = 0$ are quadratic in $b^x$; reject any root that requires $b^x \le 0$.
Always check for extraneous roots, algebraically or with a graph.

questions.text: Solve each equation for $t$. Round to two decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log {{N}} = t\log {{b}}$, so $t = \frac{\log {{N}} }{\log {{b}} } \approx {{log(N)/log(b):4}}$.

(b) First isolate the power: divide both sides by {{c}} to get ${{M}} = {{g}}^t$. Then $t = \frac{\log {{M}} }{\log {{g}} } \approx {{log(M)/log(g):4}}$.

rubric.point: Takes logarithms of both sides in (a)
Isolates the power before taking logarithms in (b)

questions.text: A {{A0}}-mg sample of a radioactive isotope decays to {{A1:3}} mg after {{t}} min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the half-life.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long will it take for the sample to decay to {{p}}% of its initial amount?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Would your answer to (b) change if the initial sample were larger? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $A = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$: ${{A1:3}} = {{A0}}\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{ {{t}} }{h}}$, so ${{r}} = 0.5^{\frac{ {{t}} }{h}}$.

$\log {{r}} = \frac{ {{t}} }{h}\log 0.5 \Rightarrow h = \frac{ {{t}}\log 0.5}{\log {{r}} } \approx {{hl:3}}$ min.

(b) {{p}}% remains: $\frac{ {{p}} }{100} = 0.5^{\frac{t}{ {{hl:3}} }}$, so $t = \frac{ {{hl:3}}\log({{p/100}})}{\log 0.5} \approx {{hl*log(p/100)/log(0.5):3}}$ min.

(c) No. The time depends only on the **fraction** remaining ($A/A_0$); $A_0$ cancels when you divide both sides by it.

rubric.point: Isolates the power and takes logarithms
Sets up (b) with the fraction remaining

questions.text: Polonium-218 decays according to $A(t) = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{3.1}}$, where $t$ is in minutes. A sample starts at {{A0}} mg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How much remains after {{s}} s?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long until 10% of the sample remains?

questions.text: Solve ${{b}}^x = {{c}}^{x-1}$. Leave your answer in exact form, then give a decimal approximation to three decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Decimal approximation of $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
Take logarithms: $x\log {{b}} = (x-1)\log {{c}}$.

Expand: $x\log {{b}} = x\log {{c}} - \log {{c}}$.

Collect: $x\log {{c}} - x\log {{b}} = \log {{c}}$, so $x(\log {{c}} - \log {{b}}) = \log {{c}}$.

Exact: $x = \dfrac{\log {{c}} }{\log {{c}} - \log {{b}} }$. Decimal: $x \approx {{log(c)/(log(c)-log(b)):4}}$.

rubric.point: Takes logarithms and applies the power law

questions.text: Solve ${{a}}^{2x-1} = {{c}}^{x+2}$ algebraically. Give an exact expression for $x$ and an approximation to two decimal places. Then describe how you would verify the root with graphing technology.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Decimal value of $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
$(2x-1)\log {{a}} = (x+2)\log {{c}}$

$2x\log {{a}} - \log {{a}} = x\log {{c}} + 2\log {{c}}$

$x(2\log {{a}} - \log {{c}}) = 2\log {{c}} + \log {{a}}$

$$x = \frac{2\log {{c}} + \log {{a}} }{2\log {{a}} - \log {{c}} } \approx {{(2*log(c)+log(a))/(2*log(a)-log(c)):4}}$$

Verify: graph $y_1 = {{a}}^{2x-1}$ and $y_2 = {{c}}^{x+2}$ and use *Intersect*; the x-coordinate should be about {{(2*log(c)+log(a))/(2*log(a)-log(c)):3}}.

rubric.point: Takes logarithms and applies the power law to both sides

questions.text: Consider the equation ${{b}}^{2x} + {{p-q}}({{b}}^x) - {{p*q}} = 0$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the equation in the form $az^2 + bz + c = 0$ where $z = {{b}}^x$, and identify $a$, $b$ and $c$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve for $z$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve for $x$ and identify any extraneous roots.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let $z = {{b}}^x$: $z^2 + {{p-q}}z - {{p*q}} = 0$, with $a = 1$, $b = {{p-q}}$, $c = -{{p*q}}$.

(b) Factor: $(z + {{p}})(z - {{q}}) = 0$, so $z = -{{p}}$ or $z = {{q}}$.

(c) ${{b}}^x = {{q}} = {{b}}^{ {{k}} }$ gives $x = {{k}}$. ${{b}}^x = -{{p}}$ is impossible because ${{b}}^x > 0$; this root is extraneous.

rubric.point: Rewrites the equation as a quadratic in z = b^x and identifies coefficients
Converts the valid z back to x
Rejects the negative z with a reason

questions.text: Solve ${{b}}^{2x} - {{c}}({{b}}^x) - {{d}} = 0$. Identify any extraneous roots and give the solution correct to three decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve for $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
Let $z = {{b}}^x$: $z^2 - {{c}}z - {{d}} = 0$. This does not factor nicely, so use the quadratic formula:

$$z = \frac{ {{c}} \pm\sqrt{ {{c*c}} + {{4*d}} } }{2} = \frac{ {{c}}\pm\sqrt{ {{c*c+4*d}} } }{2}$$

$z_1 \approx {{(c+sqrt(c*c+4*d))/2:4}}$ and $z_2 \approx {{(c-sqrt(c*c+4*d))/2:4}}$.

$z_2 < 0$, and ${{b}}^x$ is always positive, so $z_2$ is extraneous.

${{b}}^x = {{(c+sqrt(c*c+4*d))/2:4}} \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log {{(c+sqrt(c*c+4*d))/2:4}} }{\log {{b}} } \approx {{log((c+sqrt(c*c+4*d))/2)/log(b):4}}$

rubric.point: Substitutes z = b^x to obtain a quadratic
Rejects the negative root with a reason

questions.text: Solve $2^x - 2^{-x} = {{k}}$ algebraically. Explain why the equation has exactly one solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve for $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
Multiply both sides by $2^x$: $2^{2x} - 1 = {{k}}(2^x)$. Let $z = 2^x$:

$$z^2 - {{k}}z - 1 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; z = \frac{ {{k}}\pm\sqrt{ {{k*k+4}} } }{2}$$

Since $\sqrt{ {{k*k+4}} } > {{k}}$, the root with the minus sign is negative and is extraneous ($2^x > 0$).

$2^x = \frac{ {{k}}+\sqrt{ {{k*k+4}} } }{2} \approx {{(k+sqrt(k*k+4))/2:4}}$, so $x = \frac{\log {{(k+sqrt(k*k+4))/2:4}} }{\log 2} \approx {{log((k+sqrt(k*k+4))/2)/log(2):4}}$.

Exactly one solution: only one value of $z$ is positive, and $2^x = z$ has exactly one solution for each positive $z$.

rubric.point: Explains why there is exactly one solution

questions.text: Solve $4^x = {{s-t}} + {{s*t}}(4^{-x})$. Check for extraneous roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve for $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
Multiply both sides by $4^x$: $4^{2x} = {{s-t}}(4^x) + {{s*t}}$.

Let $z = 4^x$: $z^2 - {{s-t}}z - {{s*t}} = 0$, so $(z - {{s}})(z + {{t}}) = 0$.

$z = -{{t}}$ is extraneous because $4^x > 0$.

$4^x = {{s}} \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log {{s}} }{\log 4} \approx {{log(s)/log(4):4}}$.

Check: $4^{ {{log(s)/log(4):4}} } \approx {{s}}$ and ${{s-t}} + {{s*t}}\cdot\frac{1}{ {{s}} } = {{s-t}} + {{t}} = {{s}}$ ✓.

rubric.point: Multiplies by 4^x to clear the negative exponent
Writes and factors the quadratic in z

questions.text: Does the equation $4^{2x} + {{p}}(4^x) + {{q}} = 0$ have any real solutions? Justify your answer in **two different ways**.
questions.modelAnswer:
No real solutions.

**Method 1 (signs):** $4^{2x} > 0$ and ${{p}}(4^x) > 0$ for all real $x$, and ${{q}} > 0$, so the left side is always greater than {{q}} and can never equal 0.

**Method 2 (quadratic form):** with $z = 4^x$, $z^2 + {{p}}z + {{q}} = 0$. Its roots (if real) are both negative because their sum $-{{p}}$ is negative and their product ${{q}}$ is positive — and $4^x$ can never be negative. (If the discriminant ${{p*p-4*q}}$ is negative, there are no real $z$ at all.)

A graph of $y = 4^{2x} + {{p}}(4^x) + {{q}}$ lies entirely above the x-axis.

rubric.point: States there are no real solutions
First justification (signs of the terms or a graph)
Second justification (quadratic in z with negative or non-real roots)

questions.text: A car bought for {{V0}} dollars has value $V(t) = {{V0}}\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{ {{h}} }}$ after $t$ years.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long until it is worth one quarter of its purchase price?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long until it is worth 10% of its purchase price?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the number {{h}} means in this model.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) One quarter remains: $\frac14 = \left(\frac12\right)^{\frac t{ {{h}} }}$. Since $\frac14 = \left(\frac12\right)^2$, $\frac{t}{ {{h}} } = 2$ and $t = {{2*h}}$ years.

(b) $0.1 = 0.5^{\frac t{ {{h}} }} \Rightarrow t = \frac{ {{h}}\log 0.1}{\log 0.5} \approx {{h*log(0.1)/log(0.5):3}}$ years.

(c) Each half-life the value halves; after $t = {{h}}$ years the car is worth {{V0/2}} dollars. The value approaches 0 but never reaches it.

rubric.point: (a) uses a common base or logarithms correctly
(b) sets up and isolates the power

questions.text: The probability, $P$ (as a decimal), that a person will respond to a TV advertisement is modelled by $P(n) = 1 - 2^{-0.05n}$, where $n$ is the number of days since the ad began. After how many days is the probability greater than {{100*p:2}}%?

parts.label: a
parts.text: Value of $n$ where $P$ equals the target (two decimal places).

questions.modelAnswer:
Solve $1 - 2^{-0.05n} = {{p}}$: $2^{-0.05n} = {{1-p:2}}$.

$-0.05n\log 2 = \log {{1-p:2}}$, so $n = \frac{\log {{1-p:2}} }{-0.05\log 2} \approx {{-log(1-p)/(0.05*log(2)):3}}$.

As $n$ increases, $2^{-0.05n}$ decreases, so $P$ increases. The probability is greater than {{100*p:2}}% after about {{-log(1-p)/(0.05*log(2)):3}} days, i.e. from day {{ceil(-log(1-p)/(0.05*log(2)))}} onward.

rubric.point: Sets P equal to the target and isolates the power
Takes logarithms and applies the power law
Interprets the inequality and gives a whole-day answer

questions.text: **Chapter problem.** A guitar holds a note according to $I(t) = I_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{ {{h}} }}$, where $I$ is the intensity after $t$ seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long until the intensity is half its initial value?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How long until it is 10% of its initial value?

parts.label: c
parts.text: If the guitar's sustain is improved, how would the equation and the graph change?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Half: $t = {{h}}$ s, since $\left(\frac12\right)^1 = \frac12$.

(b) $0.1 = 0.5^{\frac t{ {{h}} }} \Rightarrow t = \frac{ {{h}}\log 0.1}{\log 0.5} \approx {{h*log(0.1)/log(0.5):3}}$ s.

(c) Better sustain means the note lasts longer, so the half-life ({{h}} in the equation) increases. The graph still starts at $I_0$ but decays more slowly — it is stretched horizontally away from the vertical axis.

rubric.point: (c) explains the change to the equation
(c) explains the change to the graph

questions.text: A video is posted online. {{A}} people see it on the first day, and the number of viewers doubles each day: $N_1 = {{A}}(2)^t$. {{D}} days later a second video revealing the first as a hoax is posted; {{B}} people see it on its first day, and this number triples each day: $N_2 = {{B}}(3)^{t-{{D}}}$, where $t$ is days after the first video was posted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Solve for $t$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does your solution mean?

parts.label: c
parts.text: How could you check your answer with graphing technology?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{A}}(2)^t = {{B}}(3)^{t-{{D}}}$.

$\log {{A}} + t\log 2 = \log {{B}} + (t-{{D}})\log 3$

$t(\log 3 - \log 2) = \log {{A}} - \log {{B}} + {{D}}\log 3$

$$t = \frac{\log {{A}} - \log {{B}} + {{D}}\log 3}{\log 3 - \log 2} \approx {{(log(A)-log(B)+D*log(3))/(log(3)-log(2)):3}}$$

(b) About {{(log(A)-log(B)+D*log(3))/(log(3)-log(2)):3}} days after the first video appears, both videos are seen by the same number of people on that day; after that, the debunking video reaches more viewers per day.

(c) Graph $y_1 = {{A}}(2)^x$ and $y_2 = {{B}}(3)^{x-{{D}}}$; the intersection's x-coordinate should match.

rubric.point: Takes logarithms and applies product and power laws

questions.text: Platinum-197 undergoes beta decay to become stable gold-197. Its half-life is 20 h. How long would it take to turn {{p}}% of a 1-kg sample of platinum-197 into gold? Do you think this is a viable get-rich-quick scheme? Explain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Time required.

questions.modelAnswer:
If {{p}}% becomes gold, {{100-p}}% of the platinum remains: $\frac{ {{100-p}} }{100} = 0.5^{\frac t{20}}$.

$t = \frac{20\log({{(100-p)/100}})}{\log 0.5} \approx {{20*log((100-p)/100)/log(0.5):3}}$ h.

Not viable: platinum is itself extremely valuable (and platinum-197 is not found in nature — it must be produced in a nuclear reactor at great cost), so turning it into gold gains little or nothing. Any sensible economic or practical argument is acceptable.

rubric.point: Recognises that the remaining fraction is 1 − p/100
Correct equation and use of logarithms

questions.text:
The steps of the solution to $5^{3x} = 4^{x+1}$ are given below **out of order**.

* $x(3\log5 - \log4) = \log4$
* $5^{3x} = 4^{x+1}$
* $3x\log5 - x\log4 = \log4$
* $\log5^{3x} = \log4^{x+1}$
* $3x\log5 = (x+1)\log4$
* $3x\log5 = x\log4 + \log4$
* $x = \dfrac{\log4}{3\log5 - \log4}$

Rewrite the solution in the correct order, write a brief explanation beside each step, and evaluate $x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Value of $x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
1. $5^{3x} = 4^{x+1}$ — given.
2. $\log5^{3x} = \log4^{x+1}$ — take the common logarithm of both sides.
3. $3x\log5 = (x+1)\log4$ — power law of logarithms.
4. $3x\log5 = x\log4 + \log4$ — distributive property.
5. $3x\log5 - x\log4 = \log4$ — collect the x-terms on one side.
6. $x(3\log5 - \log4) = \log4$ — factor out $x$.
7. $x = \dfrac{\log4}{3\log5 - \log4} \approx 0.274$ — divide.

questions.text: Answer each question about extraneous roots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is an extraneous root?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How can extraneous roots be identified?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give an example of an extraneous root for an exponential equation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Why can solving an exponential equation in quadratic form produce extraneous roots?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) An extraneous root is a value produced by the solving process that does not satisfy the original equation.

(b) Substitute each root into the original equation, check whether any expression would require a positive power to be negative or zero, or graph both sides and count intersections.

(c) Example: $2^{2x} + 2^x - 6 = 0$ gives $(2^x + 3)(2^x - 2) = 0$. The root from $2^x = -3$ is extraneous because $2^x > 0$.

(d) Multiplying both sides by an expression containing the variable (such as $2^x$) or substituting $z = b^x$ creates an equation whose solutions are not all allowed in the original. Every root must therefore be checked.

questions.text: Refer to the radioactive decay equation $A(t) = A_0\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac th}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Why does the equation contain the factor $\frac12$?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What does the exponent $\frac th$ represent?

parts.label: c
parts.text: What fraction of the sample remains after three half-lives?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write a similar model for a quantity that doubles every $d$ hours.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The factor $\frac12$ appears because the definition of half-life is the time for the amount to become **half** of what it was.

(b) $\frac th$ counts how many half-lives have passed. At $t = h$ the exponent is 1 and $A = \frac12A_0$; at $t = 2h$ it is 2 and $A = \frac14A_0$.

(c) At $t = 3h$, $A = \frac18 A_0 = 12.5\%$ of $A_0$.

(d) For a quantity that doubles every $d$ units of time, $N(t) = N_0(2)^{\frac td}$.

rubric.point: (b) explains t/h as the number of half-lives

questions.text: A {{m0}}-mg sample of bismuth-214 decays to {{m1}} mg in 3 min.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the half-life of bismuth-214.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the function for the amount remaining and describe its graph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How would the graph change if the half-life were shorter? Longer?

parts.label: d
parts.text: How would the graph change if the initial sample were greater? Less?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{m1/m0:3}} = 0.5^{\frac3h} \Rightarrow h = \frac{3\log0.5}{\log {{m1/m0:3}} } \approx {{3*log(0.5)/log(m1/m0):3}}$ min.

(b) $A(t) = {{m0}}\left(\frac12\right)^{\frac{t}{ {{3*log(0.5)/log(m1/m0):3}} }}$: it starts at (0, {{m0}}), halves every {{3*log(0.5)/log(m1/m0):3}} min, and approaches the horizontal asymptote $A = 0$.

(c) A shorter half-life makes the graph fall more steeply; a longer half-life makes it fall more gently. (The decay is faster or slower.)

(d) A larger initial sample stretches the graph vertically (higher A-intercept); a smaller sample compresses it. The half-life is unchanged.

rubric.point: Writes the decay function and describes its key features
Explains the effect of a shorter and a longer half-life
Explains the effect of a larger and a smaller initial sample
